title: 2  Preface
text:
Just matter of what was libido for Freud, this is my little contribution to a topic that I am very passionate about.
These notes are my attempt to truly understand how VAR models work, going into the details to see how the mechanisms behind them operate, with simple examples that make each step clear. Most of the material is based on lectures by Professor Roberto Golinelli, the Macroeconometric Forecasting (MFx) course by the IMF, and Stock, J. H., & Watson, M. W. (2001).
They may be useful if you already have a basic knowledge of time series analysis, and more specifically of AR models.

title: 3  01-VAR
text:
3.0.0.1 What is VAR?
They are multivariate1 linear time series model, designed to capture the joint dynamics2 of multiple time series.
VARs treat each endogenous variable in the system as a function of lagged values of all endogenous variables.
VARs offer a simple and flexible alternative to traditional multiple equation models.

title: 3  01-VAR
text:
Multivariate: Models several variables jointly, not just one. Each variable depends on its own lags and on the lags of all other variables in the system. (Univariate AR: only own past values. VAR: own past + others’ past.)↩︎
Joint dynamics: How all variables move together and influence each other over time — not “multiple” series side by side, but one interconnected system.
The interconnection isn’t a one-off cross-effect — it propagates forward indefinitely. Suppose inflation (\(\pi\)) and GDP depend on both their own lag and each other’s lag:
\[\begin{aligned}
\pi_t &= f(\pi_{t-1},\, gdp_{t-1}) \\
gdp_t &= f(gdp_{t-1},\, \pi_{t-1})
\end{aligned}\]
To isolate how the cross-variable link alone propagates over time (own-lag effects work the same way, in parallel), follow just the \(gdp \to \pi\) channel:
\[gdp_{t-1} \;\rightarrow\; \pi_t \;\rightarrow\; gdp_{t+1} \;\rightarrow\; \pi_{t+2} \;\rightarrow\; gdp_{t+3} \;\rightarrow\; \cdots\]
A shock to GDP today doesn’t stop after hitting inflation next period — it feeds back into GDP the period after, which feeds back into inflation again, and so on. This self-sustaining feedback loop is what makes the system truly joint, and it’s the part most often underestimated when first learning VAR.↩︎
Identified VAR: identification means separating correlation from causation — the reduced-form residuals are correlated across equations, but correlation alone cannot tell us which shock caused what. Two main ways to identify a VAR, and so to identify shocks’ effects:

Recursive ordering: impose a causal chain among variables (via Cholesky decomposition), assuming variable 1 affects all others within the period, variable 2 affects all but variable 1, and so on.
Structural approach: impose restrictions derived from economic theory instead of an arbitrary ordering.

↩︎
Impulse-response function (IRF): Traces the effect of a one-time shock to one variable on the current and future values of all variables in the system, holding everything else constant. It answers: “if variable X is hit by a shock today, how does variable Y react today, next period, two periods ahead, …?”↩︎
Forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD): At each forecast horizon, splits the forecast error variance of a variable into the share explained by shocks to itself versus shocks to each of the other variables. It answers: “how much of the uncertainty in forecasting X comes from X’s own shocks, and how much from shocks to the other variables?”↩︎

title: 4  02-From AR to VAR, usefull links
text:
4.1.1 Scalar case — the MA(∞) representation of an AR(1)
Consider a zero-mean AR(1) (deterministic terms omitted):
\[x_t = \alpha\, x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0,\sigma^2)\] {#eq-ar1}
Introducing the lag operator \(L\) (with \(L\,x_t = x_{t-1}\)):
\[x_t = \alpha L\, x_t + \varepsilon_t
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(1-\alpha L)\,x_t = \varepsilon_t
\;\Longrightarrow\;
x_t = \frac{\varepsilon_t}{1-\alpha L}\] {#eq-ar1-lag}
If the process is stationary, i.e. \(|\alpha| < 1\),1 the polynomial can be inverted as a convergent geometric series:
\[\frac{1}{1-\alpha L} = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \alpha^{i} L^{i}\] {#eq-geom}
so that the AR(1) admits an MA(\(\infty\)) — or Wold — representation:
\[x_t = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \alpha^{i}\, \varepsilon_{t-i}
= \varepsilon_t + \alpha\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + \alpha^{2}\,\varepsilon_{t-2} + \cdots\] {#eq-ar-wold}
The current value \(x_t\) is nothing but a weighted sum of all past shocks, with weights \(\alpha^{i}\) that fade out geometrically.


4.1.2 Multivariate case — the VMA(∞) representation of a VAR(p)
The logic carries over almost verbatim: scalars become matrices. Write a VAR(\(p\)) with the lag operator:
\[y_t = G_0 + G_1 y_{t-1} + \cdots + G_p y_{t-p} + e_t
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{(I_n - G_1 L - \cdots - G_p L^{p})}_{G(L)}\, y_t = G_0 + e_t\] {#eq-var-lag}
If the VAR is stationary — so that \(G(L)\) is invertible (the matrix analogue of \(|\alpha|<1\); see the note above) — then, exactly as we inverted \((1-\alpha L)\) in the scalar case, we invert the matrix polynomial \(G(L)\):
\[y_t = \mu + G(L)^{-1} e_t,
\qquad \mu = G(L)^{-1} G_0\] {#eq-var-inv}
Expanding \(G(L)^{-1}\) as a power series in \(L\) yields the VMA(\(\infty\)) — the multivariate Wold representation:
\[y_t = \mu + (I_n + \Psi_1 L + \Psi_2 L^{2} + \cdots)\, e_t
= \mu + \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \Psi_i\, e_{t-i}\] {#eq-var-wold}
where each \(\Psi_i\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix of coefficients and \(\Psi_0 = I_n\).
The parallel is one-to-one:









AR(1) — scalar
VAR(p) — matrix

\(\alpha^{i}\)
\(\Psi_i\)


inversion
\(\dfrac{1}{1-\alpha L}=\sum_i \alpha^{i} L^{i}\)
\(G(L)^{-1}=\sum_i \Psi_i L^{i}\)

\(\lvert\alpha\rvert<1\)

4.1.3 Why the Wold form is the natural home for IRFs
An impulse-response function asks a single question: if a shock hits the system at time \(t\), how does it respond at \(t, t+1, t+2, \dots\)? The Wold representation answers it directly, because the moving-average coefficients are the responses:
\[\frac{\partial\, y_{t+i}}{\partial\, e_t'} = \Psi_i .\] {#eq-irf}
A one-time impulse \(e_t\), with everything else held fixed, propagates to \(y_{t+i}\) exactly through \(\Psi_i\). Reading the sequence \(\Psi_0, \Psi_1, \Psi_2, \dots\) across horizons \(i\) traces out the impulse-response function.
In the scalar case the analogue is \(\partial x_{t+i}/\partial \varepsilon_t = \alpha^{i}\): a single shock decays monotonically and geometrically. In the VAR each \(\Psi_i\) carries both own- and cross-effects, so the responses can oscillate, overshoot, and feed back through the system before dying out — the feedback loop of the previous section, now made quantitative.
(These \(\Psi_i\) are the reduced-form IRFs. Recovering structural IRFs requires identifying — orthogonalizing — the shocks, which connects back to the identified VAR; but the VMA(\(\infty\)) form is the common starting point in every case.)

title: 4  02-From AR to VAR, usefull links
text:
For the AR(1), the inversion in ?eq-geom is a geometric series that converges only when \(|\alpha| < 1\). If \(|\alpha| \ge 1\) the weights \(\alpha^{i}\) do not decay, the sum of past shocks diverges, and no stable MA(\(\infty\)) exists — the process is nonstationary (the random walk \(\alpha = 1\) is the borderline case).
For the VAR the requirement is the same in spirit but heavier to state: \(G(L)^{-1}\) exists as a convergent power series only if \(G(L)\) is invertible, which holds if and only if all \(np\) roots of
\[\det\!\left(I_n - G_1 L - G_2 L^{2} - \cdots - G_p L^{p}\right) = 0\]
lie outside the unit circle — equivalently, the inverse roots (the eigenvalues of the companion matrix) lie inside it. It is the exact matrix generalization of \(|\alpha| < 1\): one condition on a single scalar becomes a condition on the modulus of every root of a matrix polynomial.↩︎
